title: Optimal treatment for severe neurogenic bowel dysfunction after chronic spinal cord injury: a decision analysis

Optimal treatment for severe neurogenic bowel dysfunction after chronic spinal cord injury: a decision analysis
J. C. Furlan $^{1}$ , D. R. Urbach $^{2}$ and M. G. Fehlings $^{1}$
$^{1}$ Spinal Program, Krembil Neuroscience Centre, Toronto Western Hospital, University Health Network, and Department of Surgery, Division of Neurosurgery, University of Toronto, and $^{2}$ Toronto General Hospital, Department of Surgery, Division of General Surgery and Department of Health Policy, Management and Evaluation, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada
Correspondence to: Dr J. C. Furlan, Toronto Western Hospital, 399 Bathurst Street, McL 12-407, Toronto, Ontario, Canada, M5T 2S8 (e-mail: jfurlan@uhnres.utoronto.ca)

When conservative management fails in patients with chronic spinal cord injury (SCI) and neurogenic bowel dysfunction, clinicians have to choose from a variety of treatment options which include colostomy, ileostomy, Malone anterograde continence enema (MACE) and sacral anterior root stimulator (SARS) implantation. This study employed a decision analysis to examine the optimal treatment for bowel management of young individuals with chronic refractory constipation in the setting of chronic SCI.

A decision analysis was created to compare the four surgical strategies using baseline analysis, one-way and two-way sensitivity analyses, ‘worst scenario’ and ‘best scenario’ sensitivity analyses, and probabilistic sensitivity analyses. Quality-adjusted life expectancy (QALE) was the primary outcome.

The baseline analysis indicated that patients who underwent the MACE procedure had the highest QALE value compared with the other interventions. Sensitivity analyses showed that these results were robust.

The MACE procedure may provide the best long-term outcome in terms of the probability of improving bowel function, reducing complication rates and the incidence of autonomic dysreflexia, and being congruent with patients' preferences. The analysis was sensitive to changes in assumptions about quality of life/utility, and thus the results could change if more specific estimates of utility became available.

Spinal cord injury (SCI), with an annual incidence of 15 to 40 cases per million population, has a significant health and social impact worldwide $^{1}$ . This injury is most common in young, healthy individuals in whom there is currently no treatment option for restoring spinal cord function below the level of injury. The cost of treatment and rehabilitation in the USA for every person with cervical SCI is estimated to be US 5·6 million $^{2}$ .

In addition to motor and sensory impairments, patients with acute traumatic SCI usually develop autonomic dysfunctions, including cardiovascular, sexual, bladder and
bowel problems. Neurogenic bowel dysfunction is one of the major sequelae of SCI and has a considerable impact on quality of life $^{3}$ ; it occurs in 20–90 per cent of individuals in the chronic stage following traumatic SCI $^{4-6}$ .

The intestinal pattern in patients with cervical SCI is characterized by an ‘upper motor neurone bowel’, which is frequently accompanied by constipation and rarely by faecal incontinence $^{6}$ . Individuals with SCI at level T1 or above may develop a ‘spastic’ upper motor neurone colon as a result of excessive tone in the colonic wall and anus $^{7}$ . Loss of supraspinal control of the parasympathetic innervation in the distal portion of transverse colon, descending colon, rectum and anus is typically reflected

in prolonged mouth-to-caecum transit. In the long term, development of megacolon can aggravate the symptoms and increase the risks of complications related to chronic constipation $^{8}$ . Further, visceral stimulation from the gastrointestinal tract can trigger episodes of autonomic dysreflexia in 43 per cent of patients with chronic SCI $^{4}$ . This severe form of autonomic dysfunction is characterized by sudden hypertensive episodes, usually accompanied by bradycardia and symptoms such as throbbing headache, facial flush, piloerection, sweating and coolness caudal to the level of the injury $^{9,10}$ . Loss of supraspinal control over the sympathetic innervation of the cardiovascular system caudal to the injury level (T6 or above) is the underlying mechanism for this potentially life-threatening clinical condition $^{9,11}$ . Effective bowel care is, therefore, essential to minimize the consequences of this cardiovascular complication and to improve the quality of life of individuals with SCI.
At present, clinical practice guidelines for neurogenic bowel management in adults with acute SCI recommend conservative management including diet, fluid intake, medication and local manoeuvres to stimulate defaecation $^{12}$ . When these measures fail, an enterostomy is usually considered next $^{12,13}$ . However, at least two other surgical interventions can improve bowel function in the SCI population: the sacral anterior root stimulator (SARS), which is implanted surgically (Fig. 1) $^{14}$ ; and the Malone anterograde continence enema (MACE), a procedure in which a continent appendicocacostomy is performed to allow for intermittent catheterization of the caecum (Fig. 2) $^{15}$ .
Although bowel function usually deteriorates over time, most patients with poor bowel function can be identified within the first year following SCI; this suggests a role for early interventions such as enterostomy, the MACE procedure or SARS implantation $^{16,17}$ . Using a clinical decision analysis approach, this study sought to determine the best treatment options for bowel management of young individuals in the chronic stage of traumatic cervical SCI with severe constipation refractory to conservative clinical management at 1 year after the injury.
Methods
Information from systematic reviews, utilities catalogues and a previously reported life-table were included in the decision analysis to compare the four surgical strategies for bowel care after failure of conservative clinical management: colostomy, ileostomy, the MACE procedure and SARS implantation (Fig. 3). To understand the decision-making process modeled in this study, it is essential to first grasp the concept of **utility**. In health economics and decision analysis, utility is a numerical score that represents the value or preference a patient places on a specific health state. It is typically scaled from 0 to 1, where 0 represents the worst possible health state (equivalent to death) and 1 represents perfect health. Think of utility as a "quality of life" dial: the higher the number, the better the patient feels and functions. The table above lists the specific utility scores assigned to various health states relevant to patients with spinal cord injuries (SCI).

A critical component of this table is the **Threshold** column. This value indicates the point at which the decision regarding a treatment strategy would change. In other words, if the true utility of a health state were higher or lower than this threshold, the recommended optimal treatment might switch from one option to another. When you see "NS" (Not Significant) in this column, it means that the utility value for that specific health state is not a "tipping point." Even if the actual utility were slightly different from the estimated value, it would not be enough to change the final recommendation. This tells us that the model is robust with respect to these specific variables; the conclusion holds firm regardless of minor variations in how patients value these states.

The sources cited, such as **Tufts-NEMC** and **HODaR**, refer to the specific studies or databases from which these utility values were derived. For instance, "HODaR" likely refers to a specific health outcomes database or study focused on related conditions, while "Tufts-NEMC" points to data from the New England Medical Center. Using established, peer-reviewed sources ensures that the model is grounded in real-world patient preferences rather than arbitrary guesses.

To understand the calculations in this table, we must first appreciate the concept of **Quality-Adjusted Life Expectancy (QALE)**. In clinical decision analysis, we don't just count how long a patient lives; we also weigh *how well* they live during that time. This is done by multiplying the probability of a specific health state (its "utility") by the expected duration of that state (life expectancy).

The table below breaks down the QALE for every possible combination of outcomes in the model. Each row represents a unique "branch" of the decision tree, defined by four key factors:
1.  **Treatment Response:** Did the patient receive MACE or SARS, and did their condition improve?
2.  **Complications:** Did the patient experience complications?
3.  **Autonomic Dysreflexia:** Did the patient develop this specific neurological complication?

The calculation follows a consistent logic:
$$ \text{QALE} = \left( \text{Utility}_{\text{Base}} \times \text{Utility}_{\text{Response}} \times \text{Utility}_{\text{Complication}} \times \text{Utility}_{\text{Dysreflexia}} \right) \times \text{Life Expectancy} $$

*   **Base Utility (0.516):** This is the starting quality of life score for the patient population.
*   **Response Utility:**
    *   If the patient **improved**, the utility multiplier is **1** (no penalty).
    *   If the patient was **not improved**, the utility is reduced to a range of **0.445–0.877**, reflecting the lower quality of life associated with persistent symptoms.
*   **Complication Utility:**
    *   If **no complications** occurred, the multiplier is **1**.
    *   If **complications** occurred, the multiplier is **0.6** for MACE and **0.567** for SARS, indicating a significant reduction in quality of life due to these adverse events.
*   **Autonomic Dysreflexia Utility:**
    *   If **no dysreflexia** occurred, the multiplier is **1**.
    *   If **dysreflexia** occurred, the utility drops to a range of **0.508–0.990**. Note that this is a range because the severity or impact of dysreflexia can vary, leading to a range of possible QALE outcomes (e.g., 5.225–10.182).
*   **Life Expectancy (39.5 years):** This is the base case life expectancy used for all branches.

Let's walk through a specific example to see how this works. Consider the first row: **MACE, improved, complications, autonomic dysreflexia**.
*   The patient receives MACE and improves (multiplier = 1).
*   They experience complications (multiplier = 0.6).
*   They develop autonomic dysreflexia (multiplier = 0.508–0.990).
*   The calculation is: $[0.516 \times 1 \times 0.6 \times (0.508-0.990)] \times 39.5$.
*   This results in a QALE range of **5.225–10.182** years. This is significantly lower than the best-case scenario (MACE, improved, no complications, no dysreflexia), which yields **17.141** years. This stark difference highlights the substantial impact that complications and dysreflexia have on the overall value of the treatment.

Similarly, for the **SARS** branches, the complication multiplier is slightly lower (0.567 vs. 0.6 for MACE), which generally results in lower QALE values for comparable outcomes. For instance, the best-case SARS scenario (improved, no complications, no dysreflexia) yields **11.618** years, compared to **17.141** years for the best-case MACE scenario. This suggests that, within this model, MACE offers a higher quality-adjusted life expectancy than SARS, primarily due to the lower penalty for complications.

Sensitivity analysis
Threshold values for each probability were determined using a one-way sensitivity analysis. When the range and mean values of these probabilities were compared with threshold probability values, the model was sensitive only to the probability of improved bowel function after MACE (Table 4). However, its threshold of 0·022 was sufficiently lower than its plausible range (0·400–1·000), thus validating the robustness of the model. Additionally, a similar one-way sensitivity analysis was used to test independently extreme values of utilities (Table 1).
Although the decision model was not sensitive to extreme values for many of the utilities, it was sensitive for colostomy status (threshold 0·928), ileostomy status (0·695), living with MACE (0·501) and living with SARS implantation (0·957).

Specifically, MACE offers **4.77 QALEs more** than SARS (as detailed in Table 5). Think of this difference as a substantial "bonus" of nearly five years of high-quality life that MACE provides over the electrical stimulation alternative.

However, medical models rely on probabilities, and one key probability here is the chance that bowel function might improve on its own (or with conservative management) after the injury. Based on a review of existing literature, this probability was estimated to be **63 per cent**, with a plausible range between 45 and 91 per cent. This wide range highlights the uncertainty inherent in predicting individual patient outcomes, which is why the subsequent sensitivity analyses are so critical.

### Sensitivity Analysis

In decision analysis, we rarely rely on a single "best guess" for every variable. Instead, we use **sensitivity analysis** to test how robust our conclusions are when we change the input values. Think of it as stress-testing the model: if we tweak the assumptions, does the final recommendation change?

First, we performed a **one-way sensitivity analysis** to determine the "threshold values" for each probability. A threshold value is the specific point at which the preferred treatment strategy would switch. For example, if the probability of bowel improvement with conservative care were to drop below a certain number, would MACE still be the best choice?

When we compared the actual range and mean values of these probabilities against their calculated thresholds, we found that the model was sensitive only to the probability of improved bowel function after MACE (refer to Table 4 for the specific data). However, this sensitivity did not threaten the model's validity. The threshold for this probability was **0.022** (or 2.2%), which is significantly lower than the plausible range of **0.400 to 1.000** (40% to 100%). Because the real-world probability is so far above the threshold where the decision would flip, we can be confident that the model is **robust** regarding this variable. In simpler terms, even if our estimate of bowel improvement is off by a wide margin, MACE remains the superior choice.

We also applied a similar one-way sensitivity analysis to test the extreme values of **utilities**. In health economics, a "utility" is a score (usually between 0 and 1) that represents how much a patient values a specific health state. A utility of 1 is perfect health, while 0 is equivalent to death. By testing the extremes, we ask: "How bad would the quality of life have to be for a specific treatment before it stops being the best option?"

Although the model proved insensitive to extreme utility values for many health states, it did show sensitivity for four specific conditions:
*   **Colostomy status** (threshold 0.928)
*   **Ileostomy status** (threshold 0.695)
*   **Living with MACE** (threshold 0.501)
*   **Living with SARS implantation** (threshold 0.957)

This means that if the perceived quality of life (utility) for living with MACE were to drop below 0.501, or if the utility for living with SARS were to drop below 0.957, the ranking of treatments could potentially change. This is a crucial insight for clinicians: the success of MACE is heavily dependent on patients maintaining a reasonably high quality of life while using the enema system.

When we look at the overall results, the MACE strategy consistently received the highest QALE values across the base case analysis and both the ‘worst scenario’ and ‘best scenario’ approaches (Table 5). In all three of these analytical frameworks, the SARS strategy was ranked as the second-best treatment choice. This consistency strengthens the evidence that MACE is the preferred intervention.

Furthermore, the **probabilistic sensitivity analysis** (PSA) confirmed the superiority of MACE over the other three strategies in terms of QALE values (Table 6). PSA is a more advanced technique that accounts for uncertainty in *all* parameters simultaneously, rather than one at a time. It provides a statistical distribution of outcomes.

One nuance emerges when comparing SARS to enterostomy (colostomy or ileostomy). While patients who underwent SARS implantation appeared to have a higher QALE value than those with an enterostomy, this difference was **not statistically confirmed** when we analyzed the 95 per cent confidence intervals (Table 6). Notice in Table 6 that the confidence interval for the difference between SARS and Colostomy is (-3.45, 0.57), and for SARS and Ileostomy it is (-1.74, 1.06). Because these ranges cross zero, we cannot definitively say that SARS is better than enterostomy; the difference might be due to chance. However, the intervals for MACE compared to all other options are entirely negative (e.g., -8.09 to -3.15 for MACE vs. SARS), which statistically confirms that MACE provides a significantly higher QALE.

The frequency of constipation increases drastically after SCI, especially in patients with cervical SCI $^{3,49}$ . Currently, conservative management is the first option for bowel care in patients with traumatic SCI. However, effective defaecation is achieved with conservative management in only 67 per cent of the SCI population. For patients with chronic severe constipation refractory to conservative management, there are at least four other treatment options including MACE, SARS implantation, colostomy and ileostomy $^{17}$ . Based on the present systematic evidence-based analysis of the literature, the MACE procedure appears to be the best choice for the next line of therapy in people with SCI and severe refractory constipation.

As long-term survival of individuals with SCI continues to improve, chronic problems unique to this population become more prominent $^{13}$ . Additionally, the gastrointestinal manifestations associated with SCI usually worsen with time $^{13}$ . To the authors' knowledge, no study has determined the optimal time at which to consider switching bowel management from a conservative approach to a more aggressive intervention when constipation becomes severe and refractory. Based on previous studies, the outcome assessment at 1 year after SCI appears to be a reasonable timeframe in which to determine the success or failure of clinical bowel management, as the mean time for bowel habit to stabilize has been reported as 10·2 months $^{55}$ . Moreover, at least 93 per cent of individuals with SCI have a stable bowel management status within the first 12 months after injury $^{55}$ . Lynch et al. $^{17}$ also found that, after 12 months from the SCI, bowel function does not change significantly with either increasing time post-injury or ageing. This should facilitate the early identification of potential ongoing problems, with consideration of early surgical intervention in patients with poor bowel function $^{16,17}$ .

Developed by Malone and colleagues $^{15}$ in the 1990s, the MACE technique can be very useful for neurogenic bowel management in spinal cord-injured patients $^{17}$ . The procedure involves a continent appendicocacostomy performed to facilitate intermittent catheterization of the caecum. It allows individuals with severe chronic constipation to carry out anterograde large-volume colonic irrigation (Fig. 2). Bowel function is frequently improved and, consequently, autonomic dysreflexia triggered by faecal impaction is abolished.

Although the MACE procedure can be beneficial in terms of the patient's quality of life, and the short- and long-term results are claimed to be excellent in the majority of paediatric patients, it is not universally successful or free from complications $^{45}$ . In the present systematic review, only studies that focused on an adult SCI population were included, in which the mean follow-up time varied from 1·3 to 4·5 years. Based on the clinical decision analysis, MACE had the highest QALE values, attesting to its superiority in terms of improved bowel function, reduced complication rates and patient preferences. These findings might be different if the utility of living with MACE were below the threshold of 0·501. Nonetheless, a utility of living with MACE higher than the 0·501 threshold is anticipated because a number of studies have reported high success rates and significant improvement in the quality of life following the MACE procedure $^{46,48,56}$ . In addition, the two-way sensitivity analysis for the utility values of living with MACE or SARS indicated that MACE would have the highest QALE value if its utility value were higher than 0·49 and the utility ratio between SARS implantation and MACE procedure were greater than 1·16.
In 1978, Brindley and co-workers $^{14}$ implanted the first SARS device in a patient with a neurogenic bladder. Over the past

30 years, more than 1000 devices have been implanted, mostly for bladder control. Although the exact mechanism of action of sacral neuromodulation is still unclear, it has been hypothesized that the electrical current modulates reflex pathways involved in the filling and evacuation phases of micturition $^{57}$ . Often, deafferentation of the sacral posterior nerve roots is performed before implantation of the device, in order to produce detrusor areflexia and interim urinary continence $^{17,58}$ . This posterior rhizotomy also results in loss of the sacral reflexes necessary for defaecation $^{17,58}$ . It is essential to approach these findings with a critical eye regarding the study's limitations.
A potential limitation of the study involves the development of a decision model based only on case series, given the lack of randomized controlled

Ideally, the present conclusions should be corroborated by randomized controlled trials to ensure that the results did not reflect systematic bias. For example, the mean length of follow-up was considerably longer in studies that focused on enterostomy or SARS implantation than in those involving the MACE procedure.
This difference in observation time can skew results; longer follow-up might capture more complications or long-term adaptations that shorter studies miss.
As an alternative, prospective multicentre studies focusing on surgical strategies for neurogenic bowel management in patients with SCI would be of great value.

Another potential limitation of this decision model relates to the assumption that the probabilities did not change over time. It was also assumed that the utilities of all the health states involved in the studies were independent of one another, so that multiplication of multiple utilities could be applied to derive the combined utilities for each arm of the analytical decision model. To the authors' knowledge, the utilities or preferences of patients in these populations have not been measured specifically. Although there is no information on the population in which these utilities were obtained, it may be speculated that, for example, the utility of ‘colostomy status’ probably represents the utility of patients who had a colostomy for treatment of bowel cancer. Therefore, further investigation is required to evaluate the applicability of these utility values in the SCI population. In reality, the utilities may not be truly independent of one another. Patients with SCI may have adjusted to the side-effects and complications arising from interventions, and to the resulting health states. Furthermore, new symptoms may not necessarily decrease the utilities of their health state in an independent way. Additionally, the utilities used in the SARS implantation did not take into account potentially significant benefits in terms of bladder function, sexual
and control of spasticity. Thus, the present study may actually have underestimated the utilities of the SARS strategy, affecting its incremental utilities and QALE values.

Because of the paucity of data, colostomies were evaluated without further consideration to details of the surgical technique. For example, it has been suggested that there may be important differences in terms of outcomes depending on the stoma location, even though the use of a left-sided colostomy with Hartmann's pouch is probably the most commonly used approach $^{13}$ .
Despite the impact of neurogenic bowel dysfunction on the quality of life of individuals with SCI, these results suggest that approximately one-third

will have ineffective defaecation in the chronic stage. Early reassessment of bowel care outcomes can provide significant information and prompt consideration of a surgical option. The study also indicates that the MACE procedure has the best long-term outcome in terms of the likelihood of an improvement in bowel function, complication rate, reduction in autonomic dysreflexia episodes and patient preferences.
